title: MMU shadow-fault hypothesis lab notes
body:
Purpose and framing:

This doc captures lab notes and a working hypothesis for a recurring class of instability we've been seeing across a subset of our A100/RTX-optimized compute nodes: transient "shadow" MMU faults that present like ECC/soft memory errors but do not consistently map to hardware-correctable errors. These incidents often surface as: kernel oops/panic, driver-level GPU hangs with long NVMMU error strings, and intermittent process-level page-fault storms that resolve after a node reboot or GPU reset.

Why this is different from previous ECC/NVLink runs:
- ECC surges we tracked earlier had correctable error counters and thermal/voltage correlates. These shadow faults sometimes occur with zero ECC delta.
- NVLink negotiation flaps are visible in a subset, but not universal; this suggests a separate class of failure that can co-occur with NVLink issues but is not always caused by it.

High-level hypothesis (current):
A combination of subtle page-table corruption triggered by a driver/firmware interaction on specific kernel+driver+gpu microcode combinations. The corruption doesn't always flip ECC bits but causes GPU MMU to reference invalid physical mappings (TLB miss storms, repeated page-faults), which in turn triggers watchdogs and flaky kernel-level recovery. In some cases the host kernel's PF handler masks the issue, in others it escalates to panic.

Evidence summary (observations from 2029-06 to 2029-07 incidents):
- Node logs show repeated entries like: "GPU MMU fault: VA 0x7f3c... type=read > PTE invalid" followed by driver stack traces.
- No matching hardware-correctable ECC counter spike in many events (nvidia-smi --query-ecc shows zeros).
- Kernel ring buffer near crash contains page-fault storms originating from process IDs tied to our batching daemon (redwood-batcher) but also occasionally from kubelet/systemd agents.
- Repro in lab: after heavy iterative allocation / free cycles with migration between host and device memory (zero-copy, unified memory patterns) the MMU faults become reproducible on one firmware image but disappear after upgrading firmware or downgrading driver. Implication: interaction surface across firmware/kernel-driver is likely.

Lab repro notes (steps executed):
1) Node setup: Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.7.x, nvidia-driver 535.x, GPU microcode v2029-04-14.
2) Workload: redwood-batcher with mixed pinned/unpinned allocations, large KV cache (100GB), continuous mapping/unmapping at 1k ops/s.
3) Commands captured:
   - watch -n 2 'dmesg | tail -n 40'
   - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,compute_mode,pt_mode --format=csv
   - sudo tail -n 500 /var/log/kern.log | rg -i mmu
4) First signs ~ 18 minutes in: repeated lines:
   [  1097.214256] NVRM: GPU MMU fault at VA 0x7f3c2a4b0000, reason PTE_INVALID, client 0x3
   [  1097.214278] NVRM: E@0x0 -- no ECC change detected
5) When stress continued, application-level segfaults occurred and kernel invoked driver reset path; sometimes reset failed leading to panic with call trace into nvkm and mmu handlers.

Telemetry queries (useful for triage):
- ECC counters: nvidia-smi --query-account_ecc.errors (time-windowed)
- MMU fault lines: sudo journalctl -k -o short-iso | rg -i "MMU fault|PTE_INVALID|VA 0x" --line-buffered --no-group-separator
- TLB flush frequency: instrument GPU driver perf counters where available (we have a shim exposing nv_counters/tlb_flush_count).
- Kernel PF storms: sudo perf record -a -g -- sleep 120 (followed by perf script) on suspect nodes.

Short stack trace exemplars (redacted):
- driver: nvkm_mmu_handle_fault+0x7f /drivers/gpu/nvkm/mmu.c
- nvidia: nvidia_uvm_kick_channel+0x1b3 /drivers/gpu/nvidia/uvm/uvm8_mmu.c
- kernel: do_page_fault+0x12a /mm/memory.c

Differential tests we ran (and outcomes):
- Driver downgrade to 525.x: failure rate dropped by ~70% in lab repro.
- GPU microcode rollback had mixed effect: one microcode version eliminated the fault for a week, another made repro trivial.
- NVLink disabled (software partitioning): no significant improvement in some cases => NVLink is likely not the root cause for all occurrences.
- Workload change to avoid unified memory: reduced incidence significantly.

Immediate mitigations for prod (engineering-approved temporary controls):
1) Add a kernel probe to detect repeated MMU PTE_INVALID sequences and trigger a soft-fallback: throttle allocation patterns from the redwood-batcher to reduce PF storming. (PR queued: github.com/redwood/sre/pull/492)
2) Pin problematic driver versions for fleets where repro exists (fleet label: gpu-mmushadow-affected), block auto-upgrade.
3) Add alerting rule: when node dmesg emits > 20 MMU faults in 5m, mark node as quarantine candidate and trigger controlled GPU reset rather than immediate cordon/reboot.

Longer-term lines of investigation (owners assigned):
- Driver/Firmware binary delta analysis (owner: Ravi) — correlate symbols and firmware releases to identify code paths introduced between versions that change page-table handling.
- Add synthetic test harness to CI that exercises heavy allocation/free and migration patterns with an emulator (owner: Marissa) — we should catch regressions before driver/firmware rollouts.
- Kernel-side improved diagnostics (owner: Jonah) — enrich MMU fault logs with current PTE snapshot, CR3/PGD values, and process cgroup info to pin which process causes mapping churn.
- Hardware lab: run same repro across 3 different GPU SKUs (owner: Evelyn) to quantify sku-specific exposure.

Open questions / unresolved anomalies:
- Why do some faults show transient ECC counter deltas and others show none? (Is there a masking layer between MMU faults and ECC reporting?)
- Is there any correlation with host memory pressure (OOM killer invoked elsewhere) and the MMU faults? Some incidents preceded by heavy host-page reclaim.
- Are there specific kernel page-size/mempolicy flags in our workloads that increase surface area? (Transparent hugepages, madvise patterns).

Data we still need (actionable):
- Per-event PTE snapshots stored in a blinded artifact store (script to capture: /usr/local/bin/capture_mmu_snapshot.sh) — run on repro nodes and attach to ticket SRE-3421.
- Time-aligned host memory pressure metrics (node-exporter histograms) for each incident window.
- Full driver + firmware + kernel tri-state matrix of repro outcomes (matrix CSV attached to the ticket).

Quick-run capture script (lab use, run as root):
#!/bin/bash
OUTDIR=/tmp/mmu_snap_$(date +%s)
mkdir -p $OUTDIR
cp /sys/kernel/debug/nvidia/* $OUTDIR/ 2>/dev/null || true
echo "dmesg snap" > $OUTDIR/dmesg.txt
dmesg | tail -n 500 >> $OUTDIR/dmesg.txt
# attempt to read pagetable via gdb + /proc/pid/pagemap if process known
# (manual step)
echo "done, artifact at $OUTDIR"

Next experiments (priority order):
1) Reproduce with kernel 6.9 and driver 535 but with microcode variants to narrow microcode delta effect. (Ravi)
2) Add heavy pinned allocation synthetic job but throttled to see threshold where MMU faults begin; repeat across SKUs (Evelyn + lab)
3) Insert extra logging into UVM driver path that logs PTE lookups and timestamped TLB invalidation events (Jonah)
4) Run a fleet canary with change to quarantining: if node emits > 20 MMU faults in 10m, instead of reboot, perform driver soft-reset path and mark node for automated deeper analysis. Measure user impact. (SRE runbook cadence: 2 weeks)

Notes for oncall responders (short cheat-sheet):
- Recognize: repeated lines containing "MMU fault" or "PTE_INVALID" in dmesg.
- Quick triage commands: dmesg | rg -i mmu; nvidia-smi -q; journalctl -k -b -1m; ps -eo pid,cmd | rg redwood-batcher
- If > 20 mmu faults in 5m: trigger automated driver-reset playbook first. If reset fails or kernel panic imminent, cordon + escalate to SRE-runbook-2.

References and past tickets:
- SRE-3217: initial ECC vs MMU triage notes (2029-03)
- SRE-3340: NVLink negotiation flaps, linked but not identical (2029-04)
- GH issue: github.com/redwood/infra/issues/2067 (driver regression suspected)

Concluding note:
This is an early-stage hypothesis doc. The behavior looks like a cross-layer race involving allocation/migration patterns, driver handling of PTEs, and microcode timing. The immediate path is to gather richer PTE/time-aligned artifacts, expand synthetic coverage in CI to catch regressions, and reduce blast radius via fleet-level mitigation (pin drivers / soften allocation patterns) until a root-cause patch is identified.
